title: The imperative
topic: affirmative and negative imperative; pronouns with the imperative
why: After formal questions, here is the form for telling people what to do: the imperative with tu, nous and vous, its few irregular verbs, and where the pronouns go. You'll use it for directions, recipes and friendly advice.

{"lessons": ["

Giving orders: the imperative

The imperative is the form for instructions, advice and requests: \"Come!\", \"Turn left\", \"Let's go\". French has three forms, built from the present tense: tu, nous and vous, used without the subject pronoun, exactly like English drops \"you\".

parlerfinirattendreallerprendre
(tu)parlefinisattendsvaprends
(nous)parlonsfinissonsattendonsallonsprenons
(vous)parlezfinissezattendezallezprenez

The tu form is the one to watch: -er verbs lose their -s. Tu parles becomes Parle !, tu manges becomes Mange !, and aller follows the same rule: Va à la boulangerie ! The other verbs keep their -s: Finis !, Attends !, Prends !, Fais !, Viens !

The nous form means \"let's\": Mangeons ! (Let's eat!), Partons ! (Let's leave!). The vous form is for one person you say vous to, or for several people.

Four irregular verbs

êtreavoirsavoirvouloir
(tu)soisaiesache–
(nous)soyonsayonssachons–
(vous)soyezayezsachezveuillez
Sois gentil avec ta sœur !Be nice to your sister!
N'ayez pas peur.Don't be afraid.

Veuillez is very formal: you'll read it on signs and hear it in announcements. Veuillez patienter = Please wait. Just recognize it.

", "

Don't…! Negatives, reflexives and pronouns

For the negative, put ne… pas around the verb, as usual: Ne parle pas !, Ne partez pas !, N'oublie pas ton passeport !

Pronouns after the verb

In an affirmative command, object pronouns move after the verb, joined with a hyphen, and me and te become moi and toi:

PresentAffirmativeNegative
Tu le prends.Prends-le !Ne le prends pas !
Vous m'attendez.Attendez-moi !Ne m'attendez pas !
Tu la regardes.Regarde-la !Ne la regarde pas !
Tu me donnes le sel.Donne-moi le sel !Ne me donne pas le sel !

In the negative, everything goes back to normal: the pronoun returns before the verb and keeps its usual form (me, te).

Reflexive verbs

Same logic: te becomes toi after the verb, and nous and vous stay the same.

Lève-toi ! Ne te lève pas !Get up! Don't get up!
Dépêchez-vous, le train part !Hurry up, the train is leaving!
Couchons-nous, il est tard.Let's go to bed, it's late.

Learn Asseyez-vous (Sit down) and Assieds-toi as fixed phrases: the verb s'asseoir is irregular.

One more fixed form: Vas-y ! (Go on! Go for it!). Here va gets its -s back before the little word y, which you'll study in the next unit.

", "

Directions, recipes, advice

The imperative is everywhere in daily life. Strangers giving directions use vous; a recipe often uses vous too; friends and family use tu.

Directions

You learned to give directions in the present (Vous tournez à gauche). The imperative is just as common, and shorter:

Allez tout droit, puis tournez à droite. Traversez la place et prenez la deuxième rue à gauche.Go straight ahead, then turn right. Cross the square and take the second street on the left.

A recipe: crêpes

FrenchEnglish
Mettez la farine dans un bol.Put the flour in a bowl.
Ajoutez les œufs et mélangez.Add the eggs and stir.
Versez le lait doucement.Pour in the milk slowly.
Faites chauffer la poêle avec un peu de beurre.Heat the frying pan with a little butter.
Mangez les crêpes avec du sucre.Eat the crêpes with sugar.

Take faites chauffer (heat up) as a fixed expression.

Advice, and softening it

A bare imperative can sound bossy. Add s'il te plaît or s'il vous plaît, or use a question with pouvoir for a request: Tu peux fermer la fenêtre ? For advice between friends, the imperative is perfectly warm: Repose-toi !, Bois de l'eau !, Ne travaille pas trop !

Watch the spelling: with the tu form, no -s for -er verbs, even when English speakers \"hear\" one: Écoute !, Regarde !, Achète du pain ! But Fais attention !, Prends ton manteau ! keep it.
